subject: Environment
sub_topic: In-situ conservation — National Parks, Wildlife Sanctuaries, Biosphere Reserves

concepts.name: Hierarchy and Legal Distinctions: National Parks vs. Wildlife Sanctuaries vs. Conservation Reserves vs. Community Reserves
key_dimensions: Degree of protection: NP has the highest protection (no human activity, grazing, or private ownership); WLS allows limited human activity with DFO permission
UPSC trap — grazing is prohibited in NPs but permitted in WLS under specific conditions; rights of people can be settled in WLS but NOT in NPs
Who declares each: NPs and WLS by State Government (under WPA 1972); Biosphere Reserves by Central Government (MoEFCC); Community Reserves by State Govt
Buffer vs. Core distinction: only Biosphere Reserves have a formal three-zone system (Core, Buffer, Transition); NPs and WLS do not mandatorily have this

concepts.name: Wildlife Protection Act 1972: Schedules and Their Implications for Conservation Areas
key_dimensions: Original 6 Schedules (now amended to 4 Schedules post-2022 amendment) — UPSC trap on current vs. old schedule numbers
Schedule I species get absolute protection; hunting/trade is a cognizable offense — overlap with CITES listings
How Schedule listing affects management of NPs and WLS (e.g., relocation of Schedule I species vs. others)
2022 WPA Amendment: reduction from 6 to 4 schedules, dropping Schedule V (vermin) and merging — a recent factual trap

concepts.name: Declaration and Alteration Process for National Parks: Constitutional and Procedural Safeguards
key_dimensions: Section 35 of WPA 1972: State Government declares NP by notification; no settlement of rights permitted after declaration
UPSC trap — alteration or de-notification of an NP requires prior approval of the National Board for Wildlife (NBWL) AND the Supreme Court (via TN Godavarman case precedent)
Role of the Standing Committee of NBWL for proposals involving diversion of forest/wildlife land
Distinction: WLS can be de-notified by State Legislature resolution; NP cannot be de-notified without Supreme Court nod — a classic comparison trap

concepts.name: Biosphere Reserves: UNESCO-MAB Programme vs. Indian Legal Framework
key_dimensions: UPSC trap — Biosphere Reserves have NO statutory backing under Indian law (unlike NPs/WLS under WPA 1972); they are declared by executive notification of Central Government
UNESCO Man and Biosphere (MAB) Programme: criteria for international recognition; India has 12 UNESCO-designated BRs out of 18 total BRs
Three-zone model: Core Zone (strictly protected), Buffer Zone (limited research/tourism), Transition/Cooperation Zone (human settlements allowed)
Overlap trap: A Biosphere Reserve often contains a National Park or WLS within its core zone (e.g., Nilgiri BR contains Mudumalai WLS, Nagarhole NP, etc.)

concepts.name: Eco-Sensitive Zones (ESZs): Mandate, Conflicts, and Supreme Court Directives
key_dimensions: ESZs declared under Environment Protection Act 1986, NOT under WPA 1972 — a frequent confusion in UPSC questions
Supreme Court's 2022 directive: mandatory ESZ of minimum 1 km around every NP/WLS where ESZ is not already notified — subsequent modifications in 2023
Activities prohibited vs. regulated vs. permitted in ESZs (e.g., commercial mining prohibited; agriculture permitted)
Conflict with local communities and development projects — ESZ vs. rights of forest dwellers under Forest Rights Act 2006

concepts.name: National Board for Wildlife (NBWL): Composition, Powers, and Role in Diversion Cases
key_dimensions: NBWL constituted under Section 5A of WPA 1972; chaired by the Prime Minister (UPSC trap: not the Environment Minister)
Standing Committee of NBWL (chaired by Environment Minister) gives clearances for projects within 10 km of NPs/WLS
UPSC trap — NBWL is an advisory body; it recommends but final authority for forest diversion lies with MoEFCC under Forest Conservation Act
State Board for Wildlife (SBWL): chaired by Chief Minister of the State; role in state-level conservation decisions

concepts.name: Tiger Reserves under Project Tiger: Legal Status, Critical Tiger Habitat, and Buffer Zones
key_dimensions: Tiger Reserves declared under Section 38V of WPA 1972 (inserted by 2006 amendment); managed by National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA)
Critical Tiger Habitat (CTH) = Core area: no co-existence; relocation of communities is mandatory (unlike buffer) — UPSC trap on 'voluntary vs. mandatory' relocation
UPSC trap — Tiger Reserves are NOT a separate category like NPs/WLS; they are a management overlay that can include NPs, WLS, Reserve Forests, etc.
Buffer zone of Tiger Reserve allows co-existence and eco-tourism; governed by Tiger Conservation Plan (TCP)

concepts.name: Community Reserves and Conservation Reserves: The 'Bottom-up' Conservation Models
key_dimensions: Conservation Reserves: declared by State Govt on government land (Section 36A, WPA 1972); UPSC trap — no private land involved
Community Reserves: declared by State Govt on community/private land (Section 36C); managed by Community Reserve Management Committee
These were added by WPA Amendment 2002 to fill gaps between protected areas and to involve local communities
Comparison trap: Community Reserves allow sustainable use by communities; Conservation Reserves are primarily for protecting landscapes/seascapes between PAs

concepts.name: Ramsar Sites: Wetland Conservation and Overlap with Protected Area Network
key_dimensions: Ramsar Convention (1971): India a signatory since 1982; designated sites recognized as 'Wetlands of International Importance'
UPSC trap — Ramsar designation does NOT give statutory protection; protection depends on underlying Indian law (WPA, EPA, etc.)
Montreux Record: list of Ramsar sites with adverse ecological changes; India's sites on/removed from Montreux Record (Keoladeo, Loktak)
Overlap: Many Ramsar sites overlap with NPs/WLS (e.g., Keoladeo Ghana NP is also a Ramsar site) — dual designation does not change management authority

concepts.name: UNESCO World Heritage Sites (Natural): Criteria, Indian Sites, and Conservation Obligations
key_dimensions: Natural WHS designated under UNESCO World Heritage Convention (1972) based on Outstanding Universal Value (OUV) criteria (vii–x)
India's Natural WHS: Kaziranga, Manas, Sundarbans, Nanda Devi & Valley of Flowers, Western Ghats, Great Himalayan NP — UPSC frequently asks 'which is NOT'
UPSC trap — 'In Danger' list: Manas WHS was on the 'In Danger' list (removed in 2011); implications for India's international obligations
Difference between UNESCO WHS (natural), Biosphere Reserve, and Ramsar site — three different UNESCO/international designations with different criteria and legal weight

concepts.name: Forest Rights Act 2006 vs. Wildlife Protection Act 1972: Conflicts in Protected Areas
key_dimensions: FRA 2006 recognizes individual and community forest rights of Scheduled Tribes and OTFDs — applies even within WLS and NPs (with conditions)
UPSC trap — Section 4(2) of FRA: rights in Critical Wildlife Habitats (CTH) can be settled only after the process of resettlement/relocation; habitat cannot be declared CTH until rights are settled
Conflict: WPA 1972 mandates relocation from Critical Tiger Habitats; FRA mandates free, informed consent before relocation — both are valid laws, creating administrative conflict
Supreme Court's 2019 order (eviction of forest dwellers) and subsequent stay — illustrates the tension between conservation and tribal rights

concepts.name: Marine Protected Areas (MPAs): Legal Framework and Gaps in India
key_dimensions: India's MPAs include Marine NPs and Marine WLS (e.g., Gulf of Kutch Marine NP, Mahatma Gandhi Marine NP in Andamans)
UPSC trap — Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) Notification under EPA 1986 is NOT the same as declaring an MPA; separate legal instruments
Gap: India lacks a dedicated Marine Protected Areas legislation; MPAs are managed under WPA 1972 and Environment Protection Act 1986 — a frequently examined governance gap
Coral Triangle and Lakshadweep MPAs: significance for marine biodiversity; overlap with Island Development Authority mandates — recent controversy

concepts.name: Biosphere Reserves in India: Core Facts, UNESCO Recognition, and Overlaps
key_dimensions: India has 18 Biosphere Reserves; 12 are under UNESCO-MAB network (UPSC frequently tests the number — subject to change; verify current count)
UPSC trap — all UNESCO-designated BRs are Indian BRs, but not all Indian BRs are UNESCO-designated; e.g., Cold Desert BR and Dibru-Saikhowa BR are NOT in UNESCO list
Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve: first in India (1986), largest, spans TN-Kerala-Karnataka; contains multiple NPs and WLS — a model for overlap questions
Sundarbans: simultaneously a Biosphere Reserve, National Park, Tiger Reserve, UNESCO Natural WHS, and Ramsar Site — the 'quintuple designation' trap

concepts.name: Protected Area Coverage and Biodiversity Hotspots: India's Commitments under CBD and Kunming-Montreal Framework
key_dimensions: Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) and Aichi Targets (Target 11: 17% terrestrial, 10% marine under protection by 2020) — India's performance
Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (2022): '30x30' target — protect 30% of land and ocean by 2030; implications for India's PA expansion
UPSC trap — India's PA network covers ~5% of geographic area (as of recent data); this is well below the 30x30 target, raising questions about OECMs (Other Effective Area-Based Conservation Measures)
Biodiversity Hotspots in India: Western Ghats & Sri Lanka, Himalayas, Indo-Burma, Sundaland (Andaman & Nicobar) — 4 hotspots; relationship to PA network coverage

concepts.name: Corridors and Landscape-Level Conservation: Connecting Fragmented Habitats
key_dimensions: Wildlife corridors are not a legal category under WPA 1972 — UPSC trap; they are identified in management plans but lack direct statutory protection
Elephant corridors: 'Gajah' report identified 88 corridors; Project Elephant and the role of Right of Way through revenue/private lands
UPSC trap — corridors through state boundaries require inter-state coordination; no single authority has jurisdiction (e.g., Kaziranga–Karbi Anglong corridor conflict)
Landscape approach vs. island biogeography theory: SLOSS debate (Single Large Or Several Small reserves) — conceptual question in UPSC Mains

concepts.name: Invasive Alien Species (IAS) Management in Protected Areas
key_dimensions: IAS in Indian PAs: Lantana camara (most widespread), Prosopis juliflora, Water Hyacinth (Eichhornia crassipes) — specific examples asked in prelims
UPSC trap — India has no standalone IAS legislation; management is through EPA 1986 notifications, WPA 1972, and the draft Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act provisions
Cartagena Protocol and Nagoya Protocol under CBD: IAS management linked to biosafety framework; India's obligations
Impact on NP management: IAS removal in Kanha, Panna, etc. — success stories and methods (mechanical vs. biological control)

concepts.name: Human-Wildlife Conflict (HWC): Legal Provisions, Compensation Mechanisms, and Conservation Implications
key_dimensions: WPA 1972 Section 11: allows killing of wildlife in self-defence or by State order if an animal becomes 'dangerous' — UPSC trap on who has the authority to declare an animal dangerous
Compensation for crop/property/life loss: managed by State governments through ex-gratia schemes; no uniform national law — a governance gap
UPSC trap — declaring a species as 'Vermin' (now removed from WPA after 2022 amendment) allowed state-sanctioned culling; Nilgai and Wild Boar were declared vermin in some states
HWC as a driver of poaching and retaliatory killings — link between conservation success (rising tiger/elephant populations) and increased conflict as a Mains essay/GS3 angle

concepts.name: Critically Endangered Ecosystems and Restoration: Mangroves, Grasslands, and Sholas in the PA Framework
key_dimensions: Mangroves protected under CRZ Notification (CRZ-I category) AND can be within WLS/NPs — dual protection; Bhitarkanika (WLS + Ramsar + mangrove) is a classic example
UPSC trap — Grasslands (like Banni, Terai) are critically underrepresented in India's PA network; most PAs are forest-centric, leaving grassland biodiversity unprotected
Shola forests (Western Ghats): unique montane ecosystem; protected within NPs like Eravikulam but threatened by Eucalyptus and Wattle plantations — restoration vs. afforestation conflict
National Biodiversity Action Plan (NBAP) and its targets for ecosystem restoration — linkage to UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration (2021–2030)

concepts.name: Eco-Tourism in Protected Areas: Regulatory Framework, Revenue Sharing, and Conservation Trade-offs
key_dimensions: UPSC trap — eco-tourism in National Parks is regulated but NOT prohibited; however, overnight stays inside core zones are generally not permitted
MoEFCC's Guidelines for Eco-tourism in Forests and Wildlife Areas (2011): carrying capacity, interpretation centres, local community involvement
Revenue sharing mechanisms: some states (e.g., Uttarakhand) have local benefit-sharing models from tiger reserve tourism; absence of a national mandatory framework
Dark tourism vs. conservation: high tourist footfall in Ranthambhore, Jim Corbett — evidence of habitat disturbance vs. argument that tourism funds conservation (economic valuation angle for Mains)
